brief.head: No single buyer
brief.text: There is no single giant buyer of gig labour, Amit Varma said. Swiggy must treat its workers well, or they leave for Zomato. {124-C06}

brief.head: Train your successor
brief.text: Workers have always trained their replacements, Ajay Shah said. In the Industrial Revolution, skilled workers were studied to build better machine tools; programmers automate their own work too. {124-C07}

brief.head: Ten minutes a day
brief.text: Gig work lets Indian women, who carry most of the housework and childcare, choose how much to work, even ten minutes a day, Ajay Shah said. {124-C12}

brief.head: Two apps apiece
brief.text: Do-gooders should make gig skills universal, Ajay Shah said: language and phone skills, UPI in and out, reading English on a screen, and two apps each. {#upi}

brief.head: A 10% aristocracy
brief.text: India’s labour law, Ajay Shah said, treats a 10 per cent aristocracy somewhat well and pushes everyone else out, into unemployment or gig work. {124-C11}

thought.text: Always and always the best regulation is competition.
thought.who: Amit Varma, answering fears that gig platforms will exploit their workers

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah make the case for gig work
lead.head: In praise of the odd job
body: Amit Varma opened with a tall tale. Sipping a bourbon, he said, he built a gig app called Bourbon Company to find a new co-host every week. Every week, only Ajay Shah applied. {124-J01}
“What should have been a one-night stand became an affair,” Varma said. The gig economy, he concluded, is a strange and curious thing.
Then the hosts got down to business: the critics’ case against gig work, their answers to it, and why, as the episode’s title has it, gig work is awesome.

Gig work, Shah explained, is a two-sided market in which buyers and sellers of labour agree on small tasks without complicated contracts. An employer puts a job into an electronic system; a worker goes into the system and takes it.

It comes in three kinds, he said: capital-intensive gigs, like driving your own car for Uber; skill-intensive ones, like a hairdresser who comes to your home; and microtasks, like labelling a photograph.
## The manager is sacked
In one sense, Shah said, none of this is new. Indian towns have had their naka or chowk, a spot market for a day’s labour, for centuries.

In another sense it is huge. GPS, ratings and digital exhaust let an algorithm do a manager’s job, so the manager goes and the employee becomes an outside contractor. That, he said, is a milestone in the economist Ronald Coase’s theory of the firm. {124-C02}
“The person who invented gig work should get a Bharat Ratna,” Shah declared. Varma objected that it came out of spontaneous order: “It was not one central planner who invented it.”
## For the defence

At Varma’s request, Shah then steelmanned the opposition: lost entitlements, volatile income, no career ladder, bosses that are algorithms and watch too closely, isolated workers, and Indians paid low piece rates to train the AI that will replace them.
His first answer to all of it was freedom and consent. “Nobody forces either the buyer or the seller to participate in gig work,” he said. {124-C03}
An algorithmic boss, he argued, is more predictable than a tyrannical human one, and closer monitoring should push a worker’s pay up, not down.

Varma recast the argument in terms of outcomes. However demeaning gig work looks from an air-conditioned middle-class room, he said, people choose it because their other options, from unemployment to begging, are worse.
## A list of ten
Then Varma offered ten reasons why gig work is awesome. “Five of them are economic reasons, three are social, two are ethical and they kind of bleed into one another,” he said. {124-C09}
They ran from an easy way into the city and work that survived COVID to openness across caste and religion and the dignity of work.
In India, Shah said, the case is stronger still. Only about 440 million people work in a country of 1.4 to 1.5 billion, and only about 10 per cent have protected formal jobs.
Gig work, he and Maitreesh Ghatak had argued in an article, is an urban safety net: an NREGS for the cities that no government had to build. {124-C13}
It shares two of the three virtues Professor Kirit Parikh saw in the NREGS, Shah said: it is self-targeting and self-adjusting.
“Public goods through voluntary private action,” Varma said. Then he had one last question: “And you co-wrote that article with a Bengali economist, didn’t you?”

second.label: Microtasks
second.head: Piecework goes global
second.deck: Ajay Shah on Amazon Mechanical Turk, and India’s share of the world’s microtasks
body: Amazon invented the microtask business, Ajay Shah said, with Amazon Mechanical Turk. A worker reads a task description, takes a short training course, passes a small exam and then does the task again and again, for a piece rate of a rupee or ten rupees. {124-S03}
On the other side, a firm describes a task it wants done by a hundred or a million people, sets the exam and uploads the data. Amazon farms the work out and returns the answers.
Shah seemed to recall reading that Indian workers account for 40 per cent of the microtasks done in the whole world. {#forty} “This is just something great that has happened,” he said.

quote.text: And this is nothing short of a miracle.

second.caption: Amazon Mechanical Turk

third.head: Don’t tip the sand seller
body: Critics say gig workers who label photographs are the foundation on which AI giants built trillions of dollars of market value. {#trillions} Since the workers are paid low piece rates in India, that looks unfair.

By that logic, Ajay Shah replied, the whole Indian services revolution was unfair. American Express and JP Morgan ran call centres in India; nobody should say JP Morgan’s market value was built on the backs of underpaid staff in Gurgaon. {124-C08}
His analogy was sand. A company making ultra-pure polycrystalline silicon for integrated circuits buys sand. Its expensive output is no reason to pay the sand seller more.
“The price of sand should be shaped by supply and demand, by the price system,” Shah said. A wage and a market value, he argued, are not a meaningful comparison.
third.caption: the price of sand

p2.title: Gig economics
p2.deck: Ajay Shah defines gig work and steelmans its critics; Amit Varma answers with ten reasons to cheer

sections.label: Defining the gig
sections.head: The firm redraws its border
sections.caption: the boundary of the firm
body: Gig work, Ajay Shah said, sounds fancier than it is. An employer who wants a job done puts it into an electronic system, and a person who wants work goes into the system and gets it. {124-C01}

He sorted it into three kinds. In capital-intensive gigs the worker owns the asset: the Uber driver’s car, the Airbnb host’s house, the photographer’s expensive equipment. In skill-intensive gigs, an Urban Company plumber or hairdresser comes to your home. Microtasks are sent by firms to workers all over the world.
A delivery rider for Zepto, Swiggy or Zomato, he said, might get a flat fee plus some two rupees per kilometre, for the fuel and the two-wheeler he owns. {#perkm}
## More than a naka

This is more than an old street-corner naka gone digital, Shah argued. He went back to Ronald Coase’s paper *The Nature of the Firm*, which asks what a firm does inside its boundary, with managers and tenured employees, and what it buys at arm’s length. {124-R01}

GPS, ratings and the digital exhaust workers leave behind now let an algorithm do what a supervisor of ten taxi drivers once did. The manager goes; the employee becomes an outside contractor. The result, Shah said, is higher productivity and a bigger GDP for a country fighting mass poverty.
~ Hence his proposal of a Bharat Ratna for whoever invented gig work, and Amit Varma’s objection that no central planner did: it came out of spontaneous order. {124-J02}

quote.text: Lo and behold, what have we done? A, we’ve sacked the manager because now we no longer need the manager inside the firm.

sections.label: The charge sheet
sections.head: A fair hearing for the critics
sections.caption: the case against gig work
body: At Amit Varma’s request, Ajay Shah first steelmanned the critics, in three groups of complaints.

One is about workers: lost entitlements, volatile income, no career ladder, no job security. Another is about algorithms: a boss that watches more closely than any human, workers left atomised, rules that are opaque. The last is about AI: Indians paid low piece rates to train the systems that will replace them.
## Consenting adults

Shah began with freedom and consent. Nobody forces a firm to post tasks or a worker to take them, any more than in a potato market, he said. He would accept limits only for minors, who cannot consent. {124-C03}
Training your replacement is how industrial capitalism has always worked, he argued. In the Industrial Revolution, skilled workers were studied to build better machine tools. {124-C07}

An algorithmic boss is at least predictable. And by George Akerlof’s logic in *The Market for ‘Lemons’*, close monitoring removes the information gap between buyer and seller, which should push pay up, not down. {124-R02}
~ As for atomisation, “We are each individuals,” Shah said. A worker who dislikes Swiggy can try Zepto, then Urban Company.

quote.text: An algorithm as a boss sounds bad. When you pause to think about it, it’s actually brilliant.

sections.label: Ten reasons
sections.head: Hop on, hop off
sections.caption: ten reasons gig work is awesome
body: Amit Varma first underlined Ajay Shah’s points with consequences. People take gig work, he said, because every other option open to them is worse: unemployment, begging or a job they like even less. {124-C04}
It is the case the hosts once made for sweatshops, provided there is no coercion or slavery.
Nor can platforms exploit workers at will. There is no monopsony, Varma said: Swiggy has to look after its people or they go to Zomato, and Zomato could lose them to Urban Company. {124-C06}
## Five, three and two
Then came his own ten reasons: five economic, three social and two ethical. {124-C09}

The economic ones: gig work is a way into the city and into work; it lets workers hop between platforms; it was there when COVID struck; ratings reward the conscientious; and a village plumber can borrow Urban Company’s network instead of needing a brand on day one.

The social ones are inclusion across caste and religion, choosing your own work-life balance, and moving cities or working remotely. The ethical ones are the dignity of work and the freedom to decide whom you work for.

~ Today Swiggy, tomorrow Zomato, Varma said, like the Cliff Richard song he placed in the 1960s: “Goodbye, Sam. Hello Samantha.” He did not think Cliff Richard was talking about the gig economy. {124-J08}

quote.text: They have chosen it because it is the least demeaning option open to them.

sections.label: The Indian case
sections.head: Too few jobs, too much law
sections.caption: gig work in India
body: The overwhelming problem in India, Ajay Shah said, is that there is very little employment. About 440 million people work in a country of 1.4 to 1.5 billion.
Women’s labour force participation is about 10 per cent, he said, and about half of college graduates are not working. {#women}
So critics who prize the protections of a formal job, which about 10 per cent of the population enjoys, are not being fair. “For 90% of India, what is great is having some income,” he said. {124-C10}
About one crore people do gig work, he estimated. “It’s a good number. It’s a beginning. It is progress,” Shah said. {#crore}
## Room to work

Flexibility matters most for women, who are burdened with housework and childcare. “Do I want to do ten minutes of work in a day? Do I want to do a hundred minutes work in a day?” Shah asked, putting himself in a woman’s place. {124-C12}

Indian labour law, he said, is deeply broken. It treats a 10 per cent aristocracy somewhat well and leaves the rest out, so employers and workers alike turn to gig work. Amit Varma called the labour laws the fundamental reason India missed its manufacturing revolution.
~ Gig work also eases migration: get the hang of Uber in Patna, Shah said, and the same app will carry you to Bhopal or Amdavad. {#patna}

quote.text: What Indian Labour Law does is it creates vast unemployment in India. It pushes people out.

sections.label: The safety net
sections.head: Self-targeting, self-adjusting
sections.caption: gig work as the urban NREGS
body: India’s economists long championed workfare, Ajay Shah said: welfare with a catch, since you have to show up in the hot sun and break stones. The UPA government made the idea national as the NREGS.
Every now and then someone proposes an NREGS for the cities, with the government offering a hundred days of work. {#hundreddays} Shah fears a populist government will one day do it.
He and Maitreesh Ghatak argued in an article that gig work is already an urban safety net. {124-C13}
## The Parikh test
Professor Kirit Parikh, Shah recalled, used to say that NREGS was self-targeting, self-adjusting and self-liquidating. {124-S01}

Gig work, Shah argued, passes the first two tests. Only people down on their luck take up delivery work, and supply, demand and surge pricing set the price. It is not self-liquidating, and should not be: it is a permanent net under the urban economy, the first port of call when COVID came.
Do-gooders, he said, should make sure everyone has the basics: a smartphone, UPI in and out, the ability to read English on a screen, and two apps. {#upi}
~ Amit Varma’s gloss: “Public goods through voluntary private action.”

quote.text: There should be this confidence and certainty that if all else goes wrong, I always have gig work.

side.boxText: In *The Nature of the Firm*, Ronald Coase asked what a firm does inside its boundary, with managers and long-term employees, and what it buys through arm’s-length contracts. Gig work, Ajay Shah said, reopens that question, a milestone in the history of the firm. {124-C02}

contQuote.text: Because for 90% of India, all that doesn’t exist. For 90% of India, what is great is having some income. All the things you talked about are a privilege.

p3.title: Stories from the street
p3.deck: A professor’s three selfs, an old naka, a slum and a caste-blind app

stories.start: In the world of unemployment and a safety net in India
stories.end: Because the prices paid by NRGS were steadily bumped up through the years
stories.caption: Kirit Parikh’s three selfs
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on workfare, and Kirit Parikh’s favourite phrase
stories.head: The scheme that should have quit
body: In the West it is called workfare, Ajay Shah said: welfare, but you have to show up in the hot sun and break some stones. Only people down on their luck select themselves for it. It has worked reasonably well, he said.

A series of papers through the 1980s found significant benefits for the very poorest from workfare programmes, for example in Maharashtra. {#eighties} The UPA government then took the idea national as the NREGS. Shah thinks the basic idea good, though he disagrees with its price points.
Professor Kirit Parikh had a phrase for it. “He used to say to me that the glory of NREGS is that it is self-targeting, self-adjusting, and self-liquidating,” Shah recalled. {124-S01}
Self-targeting, because if you were well off, you wouldn’t go out and break stones. The subsidy reached the right people on its own.

Self-adjusting, because when the harvest did well, people pulled back, and when times were bad, they came. “You don’t need a government, you don’t need an official to say we’ll have more NREGS, less NREGS,” Shah said.

And in the early 1990s Parikh told Shah the third part: when India became rich, nobody would want to work at 100 rupees a day. {#hundredrupees} Demand for the scheme would go away, and the programme would close itself down.
~ “Sadly, that part didn’t work out,” Shah said. The wages NREGS paid were steadily bumped up through the years, distorting the labour market, he said.
stories.why: The best welfare lets people’s own choices do the targeting and the scaling, with no official deciding who gets help. Once politicians fiddle with the price, the programme loses the property that would have let it end. Shah applied the same test to gig work. {124-C13}

stories.end: So it's that with an electronic layer on it.
stories.caption: the naka and the taxi stand
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the street-corner labour market
stories.head: Haggling at the chowk, now by app
body: For centuries, Ajay Shah said, Indian towns have had congregation points, the naka or the chowk. Workers gather there, someone who needs hands for a construction project arrives, they haggle orally over a price, and people get a job for a day. {124-S02}
It is not a job with tenure, a monthly salary, a provident fund, labour law or an HR department to complain to. “It is just a very simple pure spot market where there’s supply and demand,” he said.
The taxi stand was the same: five or ten taxis waiting in one place for customers. “Perhaps if you’re in a bad city other than Bombay, you would negotiate a price,” Shah added. {124-J03}
~ Gig platforms, he said, are that old market with an electronic layer on it.
stories.why: The supposedly new gig economy is an old Indian arrangement gone digital. What is new is not the contract but the technology underneath, which changes where the boundary of the firm sits. {124-C02}

stories.start: This is also similar to why, for example, I f feel that
stories.end: it's an entry point to a better life for many people
stories.caption: slums as an entry ticket
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what the city’s eyesore is really for
stories.head: The slum as a first address
body: When people in good urban apartments call slums an eyesore and want them removed, Amit Varma is quick with two reminders. {124-S04}
First, their domestic help and everyone they rely on live in slums. Second, in India at this moment in time, slums are amazing, because they give people an entry point into the city.
“If you’re from a village where are you going to live, you can’t really afford to live anywhere except in a slum,” he said. While the economy is in this phase, a slum is a ticket to a better life.

~ Gig work, Varma argued, works the same way: a villager need not know someone from his caste who knows somebody, but can simply sign up on a platform. It was the first of his ten reasons why gig work is awesome. {124-C09}
stories.why: Judge a rough-looking institution by the real next-best option of the person using it, not by your own ideal. Remove the bottom rung of a ladder and you lift nobody up; you lock them out.

stories.start: In Indian society there are so many divisions, so many fault lines
stories.end: a barrier from your getting a gig because a gig economy does not discriminate
stories.caption: caste and the delivery app
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the gig economy’s quiet inclusiveness
stories.head: Dinner doesn’t ask your caste
body: In Indian society, Amit Varma said, there are so many fault lines that it is very hard for a Dalit, for example, to get certain kinds of job. A caste network, the wrong look or the wrong way of speaking can keep you out. {124-S05}
Gig platforms don’t ask. “Swiggy doesn’t give a shit what caste you are,” Varma said, and the building waiting for its dinner doesn’t either: it just wants the food on time.

He admitted that some buildings have a terrible practice of discriminating against a Muslim delivery person. Delivery workers sometimes smartly give another name at the door, he said, though they shouldn’t have to. {#nomdeplume}
~ But by and large, he argued, caste and religion are no longer a barrier to getting a gig. It was perhaps the most important of his reasons.
stories.why: The impersonal platform, often criticised as dehumanising, quietly becomes a force for inclusion. In a society full of fault lines, an app that does not care who you are opens doors a caste network keeps shut.

quiz.q: What three virtues did Professor Kirit Parikh tell Ajay Shah the NREGS had?
quiz.a: It was self-targeting, self-adjusting and self-liquidating, so it would close itself down.

quiz.q: Which Amazon platform pays workers a piece rate for tiny tasks like labelling photographs?
quiz.a: Amazon Mechanical Turk, where firms post microtasks for workers around the world.

quiz.q: Why, by George Akerlof’s logic, should close monitoring of gig workers raise their pay?
quiz.a: It removes the information gap between buyer and seller, a gap that pushes prices down.

quiz.q: What is the best regulation, according to Amit Varma, when platforms might exploit workers?
quiz.a: Competition: Swiggy must treat workers well or they will leave for Zomato.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah say the inventor of gig work deserved, and why did Varma object?
quiz.a: A Bharat Ratna. Varma said gig work came from spontaneous order, not a planner.

quiz.q: Which old Indian street-corner institution did Ajay Shah call the ancestor of gig platforms?
quiz.a: The naka or chowk, where labourers and employers haggle over a day’s work.
